title: Government Agents: AI Agents Meet Tough Regulations — Mark Myshatyn, Los Alamos National Lab

primary.label: Security, Safety, Identity & Governance

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The talk centers on compliance frameworks, governance, isolation, and regulatory requirements for deploying AI agents in classified federal environments. LANL is a national security laboratory applying AI to defense and scientific research missions. The discussion focuses on deploying and operating AI systems within federal compliance and procurement constraints. The content assumes familiarity with compliance frameworks and AI agent architecture but remains accessible to a broad engineering audience. This is a recorded lightning talk from the 2025 AI Engineer World's Fair. All claims are sourced directly from the transcript with no external verification.

summary: Mark Myshatyn, Enterprise AI Architect at Los Alamos National Laboratory, opens by contextualizing LANL's deep history with applied AI and machine learning, dating back to 1956 when scientists played Los Alamos chess on the Maniac I supercomputer, omitting bishops due to memory constraints. This work followed Monte Carlo method development after the Manhattan Project. He then demonstrates an agentic AI system that designed an inertial confinement fusion (ICF) capsule for Lawrence Livermore by reading papers, forming hypotheses, generating code, and executing thermodynamic hydrodynamic simulations on LANL's HPC assets. This exemplifies moving beyond model knowledge to letting models access and act on domain-specific scientific literature and compute resources. LANL encompasses 40 square miles, 13 nuclear facilities, and roughly 20,000 researchers. The National Security AI Office has three charges: push AI science forward by writing custom models, forge partnerships with industry and academia, and integrate AI/GenAI into operational workflows. Partnerships include the UC family of schools, OpenAI for chem-biosafety work, and Nvidia/HPE for the Venado supercomputer (2,500+ Grace Hopper nodes), with OpenAI models deployed on classified networks. Trust is central: partners must handle data ranging from open scientific data to permanently classified nuclear weapons physics. Regulatory frameworks include OMB memoranda M-25-21 and M-25-22 from April 2025, NIST 800-53 Rev. 4 (1,000+ security controls), FedRAMP, DoD SRG, CNSSI 1253, and the NIST AI Risk Management Framework. AI use case governance is still being defined during a 180-day rulemaking period. Myshatyn then details four architectural considerations for federal agentic tools. First, explainability: agents must be trusted like staff, with traceable decision paths, because LANL answers to US citizens, not shareholders. Second, build for isolation: LANL is not a t-shirt company and heavily leverages open-source tools since hyperscaler cloud services are often unavailable; vendors who can deploy in DoD impact level 5 environments gain portability. Third, build for governance: software bills of materials, open-source dependency handling, and patching plans are procurement requirements that vendors should prepare for. Fourth, keep up speed: federal service parity lags commercial regions due to export compliance law, not bureaucratic preference, so designing for speed in hard corners improves fielding chances. Myshatyn closes by framing AI as both the greatest opportunity and greatest threat to national security, citing LANL's ChemCam laser sensor on Mars as evidence of fundamental science emerging from nuclear non-proliferation work.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: LANL's AI History and ICF Capsule Agent Demonstration
sections.summary: Myshatyn introduces LANL's 70-year history of applied AI/ML, from 1956 chess on Maniac I to Monte Carlo methods. He demonstrates an agentic system that reads papers, hypothesizes, generates code, and runs thermodynamic hydrodynamic simulations on HPC assets to design an ICF fusion capsule for Lawrence Livermore, optimizing yield.

sections.title: LANL Scale, National Security AI Office, and Partnerships
sections.summary: LANL spans 40 square miles with 13 nuclear facilities and ~20,000 researchers. The National Security AI Office pushes custom AI science, builds partnerships with academia (UC schools), frontier labs (OpenAI chem-biosafety), and hardware vendors (Nvidia/HPE Venado supercomputer with 2,500+ Grace Hopper nodes). OpenAI models are deployed on classified networks.

sections.title: Regulatory Frameworks and Trust Requirements
sections.summary: Myshatyn discusses OMB memoranda M-25-21 and M-25-22 from April 2025 mandating faster AI adoption with real-world impact accountability. He reviews layered compliance: NIST 800-53 Rev. 4 (1,000+ controls), FedRAMP, DoD SRG with additional impact levels, and CNSSI 1253. AI use case governance is in a 180-day rulemaking period, offering collaborative opportunities.

sections.title: Collaboration Opportunities and Architecture Preview
sections.summary: LANL holds petabytes of internet-isolated data and deep subject matter expertise. Myshatyn invites commercial partnership to push national competitive advantage. He previews four architectural considerations for federal agentic tools, starting with explainability, before the section ends.

sections.title: Four Architectural Considerations and Closing Remarks
sections.summary: Myshatyn elaborates the four architectural considerations: explainability (trusting agents like staff, accountable to US citizens), isolation (building for disconnected environments, leveraging open-source since hyperscaler services are unavailable, DoD impact level 5 portability), governance (software bills of materials, open-source dependency and patching conversations), and speed (federal service parity lags commercial regions due to export compliance law, not preference). He closes by framing AI as the greatest opportunity and threat to national security, citing LANL's ChemCam laser on Mars as an example of fundamental science emerging from nuclear non-proliferation work.

demonstrations: Agentic AI system reads scientific papers, hypothesizes, generates code, and executes thermodynamic hydrodynamic simulations on HPC assets to design an ICF fusion capsule for Lawrence Livermore
Demonstration available on LANL's YouTube channel showing the ICF capsule agent optimizing yield with a simulated slice through the capsule
limitations: AI use case governance and AI-specific regulations still on the drawing board during 180-day rulemaking period
Classified nuclear weapons physics data will forever remain classified, limiting what can be shared
Compliance burden is heavy: layered governance across FedRAMP, DoD SRG, CNSSI 1253, and NIST 800-53
Federal service parity lags commercial regions by one to five years due to export compliance law
LANL cannot obtain certain AI services from hyperscaler cloud providers, necessitating heavy reliance on open-source tools
Time constraints limited architectural detail to four considerations rather than a full architecture talk
